items.candidateTarget: in the hands of only a few
items.sourceSentenceExact: Knowledge stays in the hands of only a few people without teaching.
items.sourceSense: Information remains controlled by a small group; a hand metaphor.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The guide’s knowledge-access metaphor is about concentration of control, distinct from competence in “in the right hands” (owner 533). New scenes use archives, broadcast production and scholarship rules rather than copying the teaching example.

items.sourceSentenceExact: Digital communication is rewriting the rules of society.
items.sourceSense: Changing accepted ways of living; a writing metaphor.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The target is the reusable “rewrite the rules” frame; “of society” is source-domain detail. Examples require a changed convention, not a cosmetic improvement or literal statute rewrite.

items.sourceSentenceExact: A flashy feature may dazzle people for a moment.
items.sourceSense: Impress briefly without lasting value; light is figurative.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The target means impress strongly. “For a moment” is an optional duration in the source and is not asserted as intrinsic; product quality remains a separate question.

items.sourceSentenceExact: Public health has changed the fate of millions.
items.sourceSense: Altered the life prospects of many people; a strong natural collocation.
items.authorEditorialRationale: Examples involve long-term health, education and safety prospects, not a small convenience. The strong fate collocation has a person/group complement.

items.sourceSentenceExact: Customers can place an order from their phones.
items.sourceSense: Submit a purchase request; a natural retail collocation.
items.authorEditorialRationale: Buying stage is precise: a buyer submits a request, while confirmation, payment and delivery are later or separate events. Command-sense “bark orders” is excluded.

items.sourceSentenceExact: Large cities pull people in like magnets.
items.sourceSense: Urban opportunity attracts migrants; a magnet simile.
items.authorEditorialRationale: Plural attractors match “like magnets”; the lesson explains singular “like a magnet” as a natural counterpart but does not assess it. This is a familiar attraction frame, not literal magnetism; focused reviewer should confirm teachable reuse rather than one-time image exclusion.

items.sourceSentenceExact: The cities keep swelling as jobs concentrate there.
items.sourceSense: Urban populations continue growing; a bodily expansion metaphor.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The source supports demographic growth. Options separate continuing figurative increase from literal ankle swelling and one-off change.

items.sourceSentenceExact: If services fail, quality of life begins to slide.
items.sourceSense: Living standards start to worsen; sliding is figurative.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The slide metaphor marks onset of deterioration, not collapse. The lesson distinguishes service quality decline from rank movement in prior owner 1156.

items.sourceSentenceExact: A clever advert stirs desire for new products.
items.sourceSense: Creates a feeling of wanting something; a mixing metaphor.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The lesson evokes a previously absent wish. It is source-specifically separated from 3901, where a wish exists before the campaign.

items.sourceSentenceExact: The campaign succeeded by amplifying an existing desire.
items.sourceSense: Making a pre-existing wish stronger; a sound metaphor.
items.authorEditorialRationale: The lesson requires explicit prior-interest evidence before amplification. It does not treat first-time curiosity as an existing desire and does not claim a purchase occurred.
